newsitem.title: USA: Justice official criticizes FBI's Jewell interview.
newsitem.headline: Justice official criticizes FBI's Jewell interview.

text.p: FBI officials made "a major error" in allowing agents to interview former Atlanta bombing suspect Richard Jewell under the guise of making a training video, a Justice Department official said on Monday.

The ploy could have violated Jewell's constitutional rights and invalidated any information he provided, the official said. But he denied that the FBI had conspired or intended to deprive Jewell of his rights.
Michael Shaheen Jr., counsel in the Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility, was testifying before a subcommittee of the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Shaheen earlier gave the panel a copy of the internal report he prepared on the FBI's investigation of the bombing. The FBI is part of the Justice Department.
Richard Jewell was working as a private security guard during the Atlanta Olympics when he discovered a backpack containing a pipe bomb in the city's Centennial Olympic Park.
The bomb's explosion on July 27, 1996, killed a woman, and a Turkish cameraman rushing to the scene died of a heart attack. More than 100 people were injured.
Nearly three months passed before Jewell was cleared of suspicion in the bombing, which remains unsolved.
FBI Director Louis Freeh, echoing a memo he wrote in April, told the subcommittee that FBI management did not feel the Jewell interview met the bureau's standards.
"Had there been incriminating statements, the manner in which they were given would have invalidated them," Freeh said.
Shaheen referred to "a constitutionally suspect advisement" of Jewell's right to remain silent to avoid self-incrimination.

While agents in Atlanta followed Freeh's orders and advised Jewell of his rights during questioning, Shaheen said they also maintained the pretense that the interview was being videotaped as a tool to train agents how to interview "first responders" to a crime scene.

The Atlanta agents "presented the Miranda warnings in such a manner that a reasonable person could have thought that the warnings were only part of the framework for the training video," Shaheen said.
"There was a major error in judgment in the training video ploy. It is misconduct but not intentional misconduct," he said.

In the wake of the Jewell interview, one agent and one supervisor were suspended for five days without pay, and letters of censure were given to two executives, Freeh said. He said their names were not being released because of privacy considerations.
Shaheen's report exonerated Freeh and top FBI officials in Washington, because they did not know of the video ploy.
Sen. Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, complained that while Shaheen told the subcommittee that Jewell's rights had been compromised, his written report did not say this.
"I do not think that you have made a candid and forthright statement," Specter said, adding that he would ask Attorney General Janet Reno to review the report.
